newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian governments seen behind telecom growth spurt.
newsitem.headline: Asian governments seen behind telecom growth spurt.

text.p: The huge growth rates in Asian telecommunications have been the result of careful government planning and incentives, industry leaders said on Friday.
The rise in Internet use and mobile telecommunications was also seen likely to continue, not so much because of strong economic growth but competitive official policies, they said.

"In the official mind, telecommunications has moved from being a dominant public utility to becoming the nervous system of fast growing national economies," Henry Chasia, secretary general of the International Telecommunications Union, said.
Chasia and others were speaking at a forum during the Asia Telecom '97 trade fair.
He noted that most governments maintained a high profile in their telecommunications sectors and played key roles in business.
"Increasing the supply of fresh capital and long term investments is what every government is after," Chasia said.
Another reason for Asia's dramatic growth was government backing of creative and innovative private sectors, he said.
Chasia added that "the private sector has taken every possible opportunity to turn land into flourishing businesses."
Some governments like Japan have also expanded their roles in disseminating information and technology.
"Central and local governments have joined forces in such areas as tele-medicine and administration," said Akio Yanagimachi, executive and senior research engineer of NHK Japan.
But Iran's Minister of Communications Mohammed Gharazi said there was a trend toward breaking down the government's role in controlling information content.
He felt that many developing countries were not ready to cope with changes to culture and tradition, and lacked the ability to rebut the big global telecommunication giants.
He urged Asia, with a population of 2.5 billion, to be more active in setting international policy so that information is not used for "cruelty, corruption and oppression."
Other experts said that although some emerging countries had rejected negative aspects of information it was difficult to control what the new information age would bestow.
Francis Larapie, vice president of government affairs for Iridium said: "Revolutions happen not because things move too slowly but because they move too fast."
He said governments must take steps individually to decide for themselves what is appropriate to them. This would iron out some missing links in Asia's information transition, he said.
